key_insight: Ly and Gong propose that deep learning’s unpredictability can arise from fractal basin geometry: starting points that lead to different outcomes are interwoven at arbitrarily fine scales. If so, specifying a starting point more precisely may offer little improvement in predicting the outcome.
problem_solved: Addresses why deep learning outcomes can be difficult to predict and reproduce, even when differences in starting conditions are extremely small.
method: Frame training outcomes in terms of basins: sets of starting points that lead to the same outcome.
Propose fractal geometry as a mechanism that interweaves basins associated with different outcomes.
Connect this fine-scale interweaving to limits on predictability and reproducibility.
impact: The proposed mechanism suggests that tighter control over starting conditions alone may not reliably stabilize training outcomes. Practitioners should assess variability across runs rather than rely on a single result.
visual_elements: Color-coded map of starting points, with each color representing a different training outcome.
Nested zoom panels illustrating how differently colored basins remain interwoven at finer scales.
Two nearby starting points with training paths ending at different outcomes.
Conceptual precision-versus-predictability chart showing limited gains from greater precision, explicitly labeled as illustrative.
paper_title: Fractal basin geometry and the limits to predictability and reproducibility in deep learning
